title: Exchange Argument Proofs
tagline: How to PROVE a greedy choice is optimal — the technique that separates guessing from knowing.

intuition.analogy: You claim your queue order is fastest. A skeptic shows any 'optimal' order. You point to two adjacent people who are out of your preferred order, swap them, and prove the total wait didn't get worse. Keep swapping and the optimal order becomes yours — so yours was optimal too.
paragraphs: Greedy algorithms are easy to write but easy to get wrong. The exchange argument is the standard way to prove a greedy rule yields an optimal solution, so you can trust it in interviews and contests.

The structure: take any optimal solution that differs from the greedy one. Find the first place they differ. Show you can 'exchange' an element of the optimal solution for the greedy choice without making the solution worse (and without violating constraints). Repeat until the optimal solution equals the greedy one — proving greedy is at least as good.

A classic application is 'schedule jobs to minimise total weighted completion time': the optimal order sorts by ratio (processing time / weight). If two adjacent jobs violate that order, swapping them lowers (or ties) the cost — so the sorted order must be optimal.
intuition.keyIdea: Transform any optimal solution into the greedy one via local swaps that never worsen it — hence greedy is optimal.

steps.title: State the greedy rule precisely
steps.detail: e.g. 'process jobs in increasing order of pᵢ/wᵢ' or 'pick the earliest-finishing interval'.

steps.title: Assume an optimal differs
steps.detail: Take an optimal solution OPT and locate the first decision where it diverges from greedy.

steps.title: Exchange
steps.detail: Swap the diverging element in OPT toward the greedy choice; prove the objective does not increase (for minimisation) and constraints still hold.

steps.title: Induct
steps.detail: Each exchange reduces the difference. After finitely many, OPT becomes greedy with no worse cost — so greedy is optimal.

code.title: weighted_completion.py
code.source:
# Minimise sum of weighted completion times:
# proven optimal by an adjacent-swap exchange argument.
def schedule(jobs):                 # jobs = [(p, w)]
    jobs.sort(key=lambda j: j[0] / j[1])   # by p/w ratio
    t, cost = 0, 0
    for p, w in jobs:
        t += p
        cost += w * t               # completion time * weight
    return cost

complexity.timeReason: It's a correctness argument, not an algorithm; the resulting greedy usually runs in O(n log n).

pitfalls: Showing greedy works on examples is NOT a proof — you must argue every optimal can be exchanged.
The swap must preserve feasibility, not just the objective.
Greedy is optimal only for problems with the right structure (matroids, exchange property); many problems need DP instead.

dryRun.input: Jobs (p,w): A(3,1), B(1,2) — minimise weighted completion
dryRun.clickMoment: A single adjacent swap dropped the cost from 11 to 6 — and it matched the p/w ordering. That swap-never-hurts property, applied repeatedly, IS the proof.
